metadata.title: Tailoring a measurement model of socioeconomic status: Applying the alignment optimization method to 15 years of PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses nationally representative Swedish student samples drawn from six PISA cycles (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015) under PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling design (schools sampled with probability proportional to enrolled 15-year-olds, then students sampled within schools with a target cluster size of 35). The authors report using Mplus with the “COMPLEX” option to account for clustering and to correct standard error estimation, but they do not report applying explicit student sampling weights (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) in the text provided. Missing data were handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) within Mplus rather than via weight-based imputation. No additional preprocessing for achievement scaling/PVs is described because the analysis is a measurement-model evaluation of SES questionnaire items rather than an achievement-score prediction task.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent construct is a latent SES measurement model built from PISA background questionnaire items (dichotomous and categorical home-possessions indicators plus parental education), not a cognitive achievement score with PVs. Missing data handling is implemented via Mplus full information maximum likelihood (FIML) using an EM algorithm, which is a model-based approach consistent with multiple-imputation-style treatment of missingness under the hood. The paper explicitly describes FIML/EM in the methods, so PV and missing-data handling are conceptually addressed rather than omitted.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses Swedish students from six PISA cycles (2000–2015), with approximately 4,500 individuals per cycle. The authors state that the final number of participants was some 26,043 across the six cycles once missing were excluded. Indicator selection was restricted to SES questionnaire items that were repeatedly deployed across PISA cycles (11 repeated items identified from technical documents), and parental occupation was excluded from the measurement model. Home-possessions indicators were recoded into dichotomous variables (e.g., desk, study space, educational software, internet connection, classical literature, poetry, art, room of one’s own) and a categorical 6-level variable for number of books (with a note that the 2000 books item used a pre-2003 7-point scale).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This paper is not an ML prediction study; it develops and validates a Sweden-specific measurement model of socioeconomic status (SES) using PISA background questionnaire items across six PISA cycles (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015). The authors first quantify change in item means over time (e.g., small declines for textbooks/books/poetry and a moderate increase for internet connectivity), then estimate a sequence of confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) models in Mplus and refine the final single-factor SES model (Model 3) using modification indices from the 2000 cycle. Measurement invariance testing shows configural and metric invariance are acceptable, while scalar invariance fails (scalar model fit: RMSEA=0.081, CFI=0.825). To enable cross-time comparisons despite non-scalar invariance, they apply alignment optimization, reporting trustworthy alignment via Monte Carlo simulations (factor-mean correlation r≈0.993 for n=5,000 and r≈0.997 for n=15,000). The study’s implication is that legacy home-possessions items can support a temporally stable SES construct in Sweden, but researchers should use alignment/measurement-model validation rather than assuming ESCS comparability across cycles. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the manuscript is a measurement-model validation study (CFA, measurement invariance, and alignment optimization) rather than a supervised ML prediction/classification task. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV-based achievement targets, and no predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) reported for an ML model. The results are presented as psychometric/measurement fit indices (RMSEA, SRMR, CFI/TLI) and alignment trustworthiness diagnostics (Monte Carlo correlations), which fall outside the ML schema’s main_findings requirements for predictive papers.
